passage:
The question of what a translator owes a text—and, by extension, what a text owes its readers across linguistic borders—has animated debate in translation studies for the better part of a century. The dominant metaphor, inherited from the Renaissance, is that of the translator as a faithful servant: subordinating personal voice to the sovereignty of the source, producing in the target language a mirror whose surface distorts as little as possible. But this model, however intuitively appealing, rests on a philosophical naïveté that more recent theorists have found difficult to sustain. If meaning is, as post-structuralist accounts insist, never fully present in any utterance but always deferred, always constituted through the reader's act of interpretation, then the dream of a lossless transfer is not merely impractical but conceptually incoherent.

The most searching challenge to the fidelity model comes not from advocates of free paraphrase but from those who have probed the ethics of what Lawrence Venuti influentially called 'domestication.' A domesticating translation effaces the foreignness of the source, smoothing idiom and cultural reference so that the reader encounters no perceptible friction. The result is a work that reads, in the felicitous phrase of another commentator, 'as if it were originally written in English'—a locution intended as praise but that, on examination, reveals a troubling asymmetry: the target-language reader is shielded from the cognitive and aesthetic challenge that the source-language reader could not avoid. Against domestication, Venuti urged 'foreignization': a deliberate retention of syntactic strangeness, untranslated proper names, and culturally opaque passages that remind the reader, at every turn, of the text's migrant status. Critics of foreignization have argued, however, that its surface resistance can become a kind of aesthetic posturing, replacing the translator's invisibility with the translator's conspicuousness—substituting one form of distortion for another.

What neither camp fully acknowledges is that the ethics of translation cannot be separated from the anagogic function that certain texts perform. A sacred text, a canonical poem, a founding legal document: each carries what might be called a surplus of meaning—a penumbra of association, doctrinal implication, and communal memory—that cannot be recovered by any purely lexical or syntactic strategy. To translate the Psalms, for instance, is to navigate not only Hebrew morphology and the conventions of ancient parallelism but the accumulated weight of liturgical tradition that has made particular phrasings normative, even salvific, for entire communities. Domestication and foreignization alike, in treating meaning as a property of the text's surface, fail to reckon with this depth. The most defensible practice, this analysis suggests, is what one might term 'diegetic fidelity': an orientation not toward the text's verbal surface but toward the narrative or doctrinal world the text projects—the diegesis—seeking to reconstitute that world in the target language with whatever means are available, even at the cost of local lexical infidelity.

Diegetic fidelity is admittedly a demanding standard, requiring the translator to possess not only bilingual fluency but deep interpretive knowledge of the source tradition. It is also, in a sense, the most candid: it makes explicit the act of interpretation that domestication conceals and foreignization displaces onto form. If translation is always already an act of reading, then the ethically honest translator is one who reads as fully as possible—and who remains answerable, in the translated work itself, for the reading performed.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The fidelity model of translation, inherited from Renaissance practice, should be abandoned entirely in favor of foreignization strategies that foreground a text's linguistic origins.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because meaning is never fully present in a text, all translation strategies are inherently equivalent in their degree of distortion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both domestication and foreignization fail to account for the full ethical demands of translation, which require fidelity to the projected world a text constitutes rather than to its verbal surface.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ethics of translation are primarily a concern for sacred or canonical texts and have limited relevance to the translation of literary works more broadly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Post-structuralist theories of meaning have made it impossible to articulate any coherent standard for evaluating the success of a translation.

explanations.correct: The passage builds toward the claim that neither domestication nor foreignization is adequate because both treat meaning as a property of the text's surface, neglecting the anagogic and diegetic depth that certain texts carry. The author's positive proposal—diegetic fidelity—is the culminating thesis, making C the accurate summary of the whole passage.
explanations.A: Too narrow and too strong: the passage critiques foreignization as well as the fidelity model, and it never advocates abandoning one in favor of the other.
explanations.B: This overstates and distorts the post-structuralist point: the author uses that argument to challenge the fidelity model but does not conclude that all strategies are equivalent.
explanations.C: Correct. This integrates all three paragraphs: the critique of fidelity, the critique of both domestication and foreignization, and the positive thesis of diegetic fidelity.
explanations.D: The passage explicitly uses sacred texts as an illustration but treats the argument as bearing on translation ethics generally, not limiting it to sacred or canonical texts.
explanations.E: The author does invoke post-structuralism to problematize the fidelity model, but the passage concludes by articulating a new standard—diegetic fidelity—not by declaring evaluation impossible.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward foreignization as a translation strategy can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: wholehearted endorsement, because it corrects the domesticating tendency to shield readers from textual difficulty.

choices.label: B
choices.text: qualified sympathy tempered by the recognition that it substitutes one form of distortion for another and still operates only at the level of surface.

choices.label: C
choices.text: strong skepticism, rooted in the view that retaining syntactic strangeness is an aesthetic affectation incompatible with responsible translation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral description, offered without evaluative commitment as one of several available approaches.

choices.label: E
choices.text: cautious approval, because foreignization at least acknowledges the migrant status of translated texts in a way domestication does not.

explanations.correct: The author presents foreignization favorably against domestication but then reports the criticism that it becomes 'aesthetic posturing' replacing one distortion with another, and ultimately argues that both strategies fail by attending only to the text's surface. This layered stance—partial sympathy followed by a structural objection—fits B exactly.
explanations.A: Overstates the endorsement: the author ultimately finds foreignization insufficient, not merely imperfect on minor points.
explanations.B: Correct. The author gives foreignization credit (it counters domestication's asymmetry) but then charges both camps with failing to reckon with the text's anagogic depth—a structural objection that applies equally to foreignization.
explanations.C: Too strong. 'Strong skepticism' and 'incompatible with responsible translation' go beyond what the author claims; the objection is more nuanced.
explanations.D: The author clearly evaluates foreignization rather than merely describing it; D misreads the tone as purely neutral.
explanations.E: The passage credits foreignization with reminding readers of the text's 'migrant status,' but the author's overall judgment is more critical than 'cautious approval' conveys, given the structural deficiency identified in paragraph three.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A historical survey of translation practices is presented, two influential theorists are compared, and a synthesis reconciling their positions is proposed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A dominant model is identified and philosophically undermined; two competing alternatives are presented and found jointly inadequate on ethical and conceptual grounds; a new standard is introduced and defended.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A traditional debate is described, a post-structuralist critique is introduced and endorsed, and the implications for sacred-text translation are explored.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two camps within translation studies are contrasted, the stronger camp is endorsed, and specific examples from biblical translation are offered in support.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An initial claim about translation ethics is stated, several objections to it are catalogued, and the claim is ultimately reaffirmed with minor qualifications.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 identifies and undermines the fidelity/faithful-servant model; paragraph 2 presents domestication and foreignization as alternatives but notes each has a fatal flaw; paragraph 3 introduces the anagogic/surplus-of-meaning argument that both camps neglect, then proposes diegetic fidelity; paragraph 4 defends and contextualizes that standard. B tracks these four moves accurately.
explanations.A: The passage does not present a 'historical survey,' nor does it compare two theorists and then synthesize them; the structure is more argumentatively progressive than syncretic.
explanations.C: The post-structuralist critique is introduced as support for undermining the fidelity model, not as the passage's endorsed framework; the sacred-text example illustrates a broader point rather than being the focus.
explanations.D: Neither domestication nor foreignization is ultimately endorsed; the passage rejects both as surface-level strategies.
explanations.E: No initial claim is 'reaffirmed'—the passage moves from a rejected dominant model to a newly proposed one, which is a different structure.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, a domesticating translation is characterized by which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It retains culturally opaque passages in order to remind readers of the source text's origins.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It effaces the foreignness of the source by smoothing idiom and cultural reference, producing a text that reads without perceptible friction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It subordinates the translator's personal voice entirely to the sovereignty of the source language.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It preserves the syntactic strangeness of the source language, making the translator's presence conspicuous.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It engages with the anagogic function of the source text by reconstituting the diegetic world in the target language.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly defines domestication as efacing the foreignness of the source, 'smoothing idiom and cultural reference so that the reader encounters no perceptible friction,' producing a work that reads 'as if it were originally written in English.' B paraphrases this definition accurately.
explanations.A: This describes foreignization, not domestication; domestication removes cultural opacity rather than retaining it.
explanations.B: Correct. This is a precise paraphrase of the passage's explicit definition of domestication.
explanations.C: This describes the Renaissance faithful-servant model, not domestication specifically; the passage distinguishes these.
explanations.D: This describes foreignization—the deliberate retention of syntactic strangeness and conspicuous translator presence—the opposite of domestication.
explanations.E: This describes the proposed practice of diegetic fidelity, which the passage presents as a new alternative beyond both domestication and foreignization.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that a translator practicing 'diegetic fidelity' would be most likely to do which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adopt syntactically foreign constructions whenever preserving the verbal surface of the source text is feasible.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Render a culturally specific metaphor using a different but functionally equivalent metaphor in the target language, if doing so better reconstitutes the text's projected world.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Privilege the reader's comfort by eliminating cultural references that might impede comprehension.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Refuse to translate sacred or canonical texts, on the grounds that their surplus of meaning is irreducibly bound to the source language.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Restrict interpretive decisions to the lexical level, ensuring that individual word choices are verifiable against the source text's vocabulary.

explanations.correct: Diegetic fidelity orients the translator 'not toward the text's verbal surface but toward the narrative or doctrinal world the text projects—the diegesis—seeking to reconstitute that world in the target language with whatever means are available, even at the cost of local lexical infidelity.' B instantiates exactly this: sacrificing a specific verbal element (the original metaphor) to better serve the diegetic world.
explanations.A: Retaining syntactically foreign constructions is a feature of foreignization, which diegetic fidelity is presented as superseding; the passage does not identify surface-level strangeness as a goal of diegetic fidelity.
explanations.B: Correct. The passage explicitly allows for 'local lexical infidelity' in service of the diegetic world, which is precisely what substituting a functionally equivalent metaphor represents.
explanations.C: Eliminating cultural references for reader comfort describes domestication, the opposite of what diegetic fidelity demands.
explanations.D: The passage uses sacred texts as an illustration of why diegetic fidelity is needed, not as evidence that such texts should be left untranslated; the author's proposal is a positive program, not a counsel of despair.
explanations.E: Restricting decisions to the lexical level is the surface-oriented approach that diegetic fidelity explicitly moves beyond; the passage says this approach fails for texts with anagogic surplus.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of translating the Psalms (third paragraph) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide a counterexample demonstrating that domestication occasionally succeeds where foreignization fails.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate why both domestication and foreignization are inadequate by showing that certain texts carry a depth of accumulated meaning no surface-level strategy can recover.

choices.label: C
choices.text: argue that liturgical tradition should take precedence over linguistic accuracy in all decisions about how to translate religious texts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that post-structuralist accounts of meaning are uniquely applicable to the translation of ancient texts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: suggest that the translator's bilingual fluency is a more important qualification than interpretive knowledge of the source tradition.

explanations.correct: The Psalms example appears immediately after the author introduces the concept of a 'surplus of meaning'—a penumbra of doctrinal implication and communal memory—to show why neither domestication nor foreignization can suffice. The example concretizes the abstract claim that purely lexical or syntactic strategies fail for certain texts, making B the correct account of its function.
explanations.A: The passage does not pit domestication against foreignization in the context of the Psalms; it uses the Psalms to charge both strategies equally with inadequacy.
explanations.B: Correct. The example is an illustration of the 'surplus of meaning' argument, not a test case for one strategy versus another.
explanations.C: The passage says the translator must navigate both linguistic form and liturgical tradition, not that tradition takes precedence in all cases; this overstates and narrows the claim.
explanations.D: Post-structuralism is discussed in paragraph 1, not in the context of the Psalms example; importing it here misidentifies the rhetorical function.
explanations.E: The passage says diegetic fidelity requires both bilingual fluency and 'deep interpretive knowledge'—it does not rank one above the other, and the Psalms example does not address this comparison.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's argument for diegetic fidelity as an ethical translation standard?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most translators already report that they attend to thematic coherence as well as lexical accuracy when making translation decisions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Post-structuralist theorists have argued that the 'diegesis' of a text is no less subject to interpretive deferral and instability than its verbal surface, making the projected world of a text as indeterminate as its lexical meaning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lawrence Venuti's concept of foreignization has been influential primarily within academic translation studies rather than among practicing translators.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several celebrated translations of the Psalms have been praised by liturgical communities for their preservation of archaic phrasing.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The requirement that translators possess deep interpretive knowledge of the source tradition makes diegetic fidelity a practically demanding but not conceptually incoherent standard.

explanations.correct: The author's argument for diegetic fidelity rests on the claim that the diegesis—the narrative or doctrinal world projected by the text—provides a stable target that translators can orient toward, even when verbal surfaces are sacrificed. If post-structuralist analysis extends the same instability and deferral to the diegesis that the author acknowledged applies to verbal meaning, then diegetic fidelity loses its theoretical anchor: the translator's target is no more determinate than what was being rejected. B attacks the foundational premise of the proposed standard.
explanations.A: This would, if anything, lend empirical support to the plausibility of diegetic fidelity as a standard, not undermine it.
explanations.B: Correct. This is a direct attack on the conceptual coherence of the proposed standard, extending the post-structuralist critique the author used to undermine the fidelity model to undermine diegetic fidelity itself.
explanations.C: The academic versus practitioner reception of foreignization is irrelevant to whether diegetic fidelity is a sound ethical standard; this is an off-target claim.
explanations.D: This is consistent with the author's view and might even illustrate the anagogic surplus argument; it does not undermine diegetic fidelity.
explanations.E: This explicitly concedes that diegetic fidelity is demanding but denies it is incoherent—which supports rather than undermines the author's position.
